source.title: Are LLMs Good Safety Agents or a Propaganda Engine?
source.authors: Neemesh Yadav; Francesco Ortu; Jia-Rui Liu; Joeun Yook; Bernhard Scholkopf; Rada Mihalcea; Alberto Cazzaniga; Zhi-Jing Jin

page_placements.theme: Category and topic structure: shared refusal component, category-specific harm parts, topic-specific (political) refusal

record.file_problem: none; the full paper text is present.
record.tranche_reason: The paper studies refusals and erases a political concept, but does not find, remove, add, or test the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction or any of the listed versions. It cites the original paper in its discussion of linear representations.
record.gate_note: The paper reports refusal rates on explicit and implicit political prompts, after LEACE erasure of a political concept, and under Cognitive Hacking. These results concern political-context sensitivity and refusal behavior, not the refusal direction or its proposed causal role. They are recorded as findings fitting no version. The paper also reports refusal-category distributions and guardrail classification results; those are not separately extracted where the refusal-rate rows capture the relevant comparison, and guardrail classifications are not refusal behavior.
record.test_reason: The study measures refusal rates on political prompts, under LEACE erasure of a 'political' concept and under a Cognitive Hacking prompt. It never computes, ablates, adds or probes the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction. Arditi et al. is cited only in related work and Appendix B as background on linear representations. No row bears on V1–V8.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly right, but incomplete. The authors conclude four things. First, DeepSeek R1 and Llama 3.1 censor by refusing content with negligible malicious intent. Second, Llama 3.1 is highly sensitive to political context, unlike PromptGuard. Third, Cognitive Hacking pushes models into 'ethical dilemma' partial refusals and can increase refusal. Fourth, neither parameter count nor country context affects refusal distributions, although Figure 3b shows more refusal for Chinese and Russian contexts.
record.recipe_differences: No refusal-direction method from the original study is applied. LEACE erases political information, while Cognitive Hacking modifies prompts.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported refusal rates vary across models and between explicit PSP prompts, implicit prompts, LEACE-erased prompts, and Cognitive Hacking prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Refusal rates on explicit political prompts (Rr) drop sharply on implicit topic-only prompts (Rc) for most models, e.g. Llama 3.3 70B goes from 32.5 to 0.94. Llama 3.1 8B keeps 26.74.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Masking explicit political intent reduces refusal on politically sensitive prompts, to a degree that varies by model.

fits_no_version.finding: LEACE erasure of a linear 'political' concept cuts Llama 3.1 8B refusal from 63.06 to 14.89, and OLMo 7B from 20.95 to 9.36.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Linearly erasing a political-context concept from prompt representations reduces refusal on political prompts.

fits_no_version.finding: Cognitive Hacking raises partial refusals in most models. It lowers complete refusal in some models (OLMo, Llama 3.1, Llama 3.3) and raises it in others (Qwen, GPT-4o, Mixtral).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Competing-objective prompt injections shift political-prompt responses toward partial refusal, and their effect on complete refusal depends on the model.

record.problems: Refusal categories are assigned by GPT-4o, with agreement comparisons to other model judges but no human adjudication stated. Political sensitivity and censorship are operationalized through the study's prompt construction and implicit-prompt proxy. No general-capability evaluation is reported. The paper describes a 150-prompt contrastive set for LEACE. Statistical significance is mentioned for some model comparisons, but uncertainty estimates are not supplied alongside the refusal-rate table values.
record.rows_left_out: Table 2 and Table 4 also give complete-refusal, no-refusal, and failure category distributions; these were not separately extracted because the rows retain the aggregate refusal-rate comparisons, with partial-refusal rates included for the Cognitive Hacking result emphasized in the text. Table 3 guardrail-model unsafe, maliciousness, and jailbreak classifications were left out because they are classifier outcomes rather than refusal behavior.

untested.parts: No difference-in-means refusal direction is extracted, ablated or added; general capability is not checked.
Cognitive Hacking refusal rates are measured, but not whether the attack suppresses the refusal direction; no adversarial training.
The study separates censorship from safety refusal conceptually and behaviourally, but does not test separate internal encoding of harmfulness versus refusal.
Training is not varied; the authors only speculate that Mixtral lacks explicit safety tuning.
DeepSeek R1 Distill Llama 70B gets behavioural refusal rates only; no direction analysis.

record.verdict_notes: The record's cites_only/T6 call is correct. All rows correctly carry versions ['none']. The LEACE intervention is linear concept erasure, which is superficially similar to direction ablation, but the concept erased is political-vs-taboo topic, not refusal, and no capability check is made.

versions.untested_parts: The difference-in-means refusal direction, its removal or addition, refusal mediation, and preservation of general capability are not tested.
No weight edit or released-model abliteration is tested.
Cognitive Hacking is applied, but the study does not test whether it suppresses the refusal direction or whether training against its ablation adds robustness.
The geometry or number of refusal directions is not tested.
The paper distinguishes political censorship from safety refusal conceptually, but does not test whether harmfulness judgments are separately encoded from refusal decisions.
No refusal-direction transfer across languages, model variants, or base and instruct models is tested.
The study does not vary refusal training or test whether training determines the existence of a removable direction.
DeepSeek R1 is evaluated for political-prompt refusals, but no refusal-direction intervention or measurement is performed on a reasoning model.

relation.reason: Arditi et al. 2024 appears only in related work (as activation steering) and in Appendix B (as another concept-removal method based on linear representations). The paper does not discuss it further.

tranche.reason: The study never computes, ablates, adds or probes the harmful-minus-harmless refusal direction. LEACE erases a political-vs-taboo concept, and the Dimp test and Cognitive Hacking are prompt-level. None of its results bear on V1-V8, and it does not use the direction as a tool.

source_check.notes: The Table 3 Δ values print with signs opposite to the caption's own formula Δ = Rc − R̂r (2.17−9.36 = −7.19, but 7.19 is printed), probably because sign colours were lost in extraction. Llama 3.1 8B gives 87.11% Failure on Dimp, so its Rc of 26.74 is computed on only about 13% of responses. LlamaGuard 3 collapsed to 100% failure after erasure.

statements.correction: Llama 3.1 8B on Dimp: CR 3.45, PR 0.31, NR 9.14, F 87.11; Rc = CR/(CR+PR+NR) = 26.74. Llama 3.3 70B on Dimp: F 0, Rc 0.94. The LEACE eraser was fit on 150 PSP prompts vs 150 non-political taboo prompts.
statements.problem: All numbers match: Table 3 (63.06 to 14.89, 20.95 to 9.36) and Table 2 (Llama 3.3 70B Rr 32.5 to Rc 0.94; Llama 3.1 8B Rc 26.74). The statement leaves out that Llama 3.1 8B's Dimp Rc excludes 87.11% Failure responses, which makes the 26.74 vs 0.94 contrast look stronger than it is.
